title: From Machinery Noise to a Sonar Track
headline: Follow the dependency chain that lets a passive array turn pressure fluctuations into a classified contact.
kicker: Ocean acoustics laboratory · A distant ship is radiating broadband and tonal sound
story: A ship over the horizon cannot be seen, yet its machinery and propeller disturb the surrounding water. A passive sonar operator receives only the pressure field that survives the ocean path.
Arrange the physical and computational sequence from source vibration to a stable bearing-and-frequency track.
overview: Passive sonar does not transmit a pulse. It depends on sound generated by a source, propagation through a variable ocean, conversion of pressure to electrical signals, array processing, and repeated observations that support classification. Each stage needs the output of the stage before it.
terms: Formation and collapse of vapor bubbles near a propeller when local pressure falls sufficiently.
How sound speed changes with depth because of temperature, salinity, and pressure.
Bending of a wave path when propagation speed changes with position.
A sensor that converts underwater pressure changes into an electrical signal.
Combining time-shifted array channels to favor sound arriving from one direction.
A narrow frequency feature often associated with rotating machinery.
A time-linked estimate of a contact’s bearing, motion, and signal features.
note: Real oceans can create multiple paths, shadow zones, and strong biological or shipping noise. The game uses a single dominant path so the causal order remains unique.
sources: Fact-checked against U.S. Navy and NOAA primers on underwater sound, sound-speed variation, sonar, hydrophones, and acoustic propagation.

cards: Loaded machinery and the propulsion shaft exert changing forces
Those forces vibrate machinery foundations, hull plating, and the propeller
The moving surfaces push and pull on nearby seawater
The resulting pressure disturbances radiate as an acoustic field
Sound energy leaves the source region
The local sound-speed profile sets how rays bend
Spreading and absorption reduce the received level
A weakened pressure pattern reaches the receiving array
Hydrophones convert pressure changes into voltage signals
The processor applies relative delays across array channels
Repeated bearings and spectral lines are associated into a contact track

segues: The source has created a pressure field, but the receiver will not observe a simple copy. The ocean path now determines which frequencies and directions survive.
The array has received pressure fluctuations, not a contact label. Sensor conversion and coherent processing must turn those fluctuations into directional evidence before tracking can begin.
principles: Trace the information carrier
Mechanical vibration becomes pressure variation, then voltage, then a directional estimate.
Propagation happens before detection
The sound-speed structure and transmission loss act on the signal before any processor can recover it.
An array needs relative timing
Direction comes from phase or arrival-time differences among separated hydrophones.
Classification follows detection
A stable bearing and spectrum provide the evidence used to form and classify a track.
hints: The hull must first move the water before any acoustic pressure field can leave the source.
Hydrophones produce channel voltages before beamforming can favor an arrival direction.
intro: The distant ship is operating steadily. Sequence A must create an underwater pressure disturbance before ocean propagation or receiver processing can occur.

title: From Radar Pulse to Confirmed Track
headline: Order the physical and information-processing steps behind pulse-echo radar.
kicker: Surface-search radar · A small contact is near the electromagnetic horizon
story: A rotating radar must illuminate a sector, receive a tiny echo amid noise and clutter, and decide whether repeated returns belong to one moving object.
Arrange the chain from waveform creation through detection, ranging, and track formation.
overview: Radar range is inferred from elapsed time, but a usable track requires much more than a stopwatch. The transmitter must create a waveform, the antenna must radiate it, the target must scatter some energy back, the receiver must protect itself and recover the echo, and repeated measurements must be associated over time.
terms: A device that alternately connects a shared antenna to the transmitter and receiver while protecting the receiver.
Energy redirected toward the radar after the wave interacts with a target.
A processor designed to maximize response to a known waveform in noise.
A time window corresponding to a selected distance interval.
Unwanted echoes from sea, land, weather, or other distributed reflectors.
A time-linked record of estimated target position and motion.
note: Real radars may use pulse compression, Doppler processing, electronic steering, and parallel tracking. The sequence shows the dependency order common to pulse-echo systems.
sources: Fact-checked against Naval History and Heritage Command radar descriptions and standard pulse-echo radar principles.

cards: The exciter forms a timed radio-frequency waveform
The transmitter raises the waveform to high peak power
The duplexer connects the antenna to the transmitter
The antenna directs the pulse into a search sector
After the pulse, the duplexer connects the antenna to the protected receiver
The transmitted pulse propagates outward at electromagnetic-wave speed
A target intercepts and backscatters a small fraction
The echo returns through the antenna and receive path
The receiver and matched filter recover echo energy
Round-trip delay is converted into target range
Threshold and clutter processing declare a plot
Plots from successive scans are associated into a track

segues: The pulse has left the antenna. A range measurement is impossible until energy interacts with an object and returns to the same radar.
The receiver now has a weak waveform mixed with noise and clutter. Signal processing must recover evidence from each scan before a tracker can connect detections through time.
principles: Range comes from round-trip time
The clock starts with transmission and ends when the echo is received.
Most transmitted energy never returns
Target geometry and spreading make the received echo far weaker than the outgoing pulse.
Detection is not tracking
One threshold crossing is a plot; motion requires association across scans.
Protection precedes reception
A shared-antenna receiver must be isolated from the high-power transmit pulse.
hints: The target must scatter the outward pulse before an echo can travel back.
A plot must be declared on an individual scan before successive plots can be associated into a track.
intro: The radar has not yet transmitted. Sequence A must create, amplify, switch, and radiate a waveform before any target echo can exist.

title: From Intake Air to Propeller Thrust
headline: Follow energy through a marine gas-turbine propulsion train.
kicker: Engineering plant · A gas turbine is ordered from idle to ahead power
story: The bridge requests more speed. Fuel alone cannot turn the propeller: the plant must establish airflow, release heat, extract shaft work, transmit torque, and accelerate water astern.
Arrange the thermodynamic and mechanical chain that produces ship thrust.
overview: A marine gas turbine is an open-cycle heat engine. The compressor raises air pressure, fuel adds chemical energy, hot gas expands through turbine stages, and a power turbine drives reduction gearing and a shaft. The propeller then converts shaft torque into a pressure and momentum change in the water.
terms: Rotating stages that raise the pressure of incoming air.
Chamber where fuel burns in compressed air.
Turbine stages that power the compressor.
Turbine that extracts useful output shaft work.
Gearing that trades high turbine speed for lower propeller speed and higher torque.
The geometric advance associated with one propeller revolution in an ideal solid medium.
Force produced by changing the momentum and pressure of a fluid.
note: Some ships use controllable-pitch propellers, combining gears, or electric transmission. This sequence follows a direct mechanical gas-turbine drive.
sources: Fact-checked against standard Brayton-cycle and marine propulsion descriptions used in naval engineering education.

cards: Intake ducts deliver filtered ambient air
Compressor stages raise the air pressure
Fuel is metered and burns in the compressed airflow
Hot gas expands through the gas-generator turbine
The gas-generator turbine keeps the compressor turning
Remaining gas energy turns the free power turbine
Reduction gearing lowers rotational speed and raises shaft torque
The propulsion shaft carries torque toward the stern
The propeller rotates under applied shaft torque
Blade sections create a pressure difference across the propeller disk
The propeller accelerates a mass of water astern
The reaction force accelerates the ship ahead

segues: The gas generator is now self-sustaining. Useful propulsion still requires extracting remaining exhaust energy on a separate output shaft and matching its speed to the propeller.
Torque has reached the propeller shaft, but torque is not yet ship motion. The propeller must exchange momentum with the water to create an external force on the hull.
principles: Follow energy, not just components
Chemical energy becomes thermal energy, gas kinetic energy, shaft work, and finally fluid momentum.
The compressor must be paid for
Part of turbine work only keeps the engine breathing; useful output comes after that internal demand.
Gearing matches machines
Turbines favor high rotational speed while large propellers operate efficiently at much lower speed.
Thrust requires the environment
The ship moves because the propeller pushes water astern and water pushes the propeller—and ship—ahead.
hints: Compressed air must reach the combustor before fuel can burn stably in the gas path.
Reduction gearing changes turbine speed before torque reaches the propeller shaft.
intro: The bridge has requested ahead power, but the engine contains only stationary air and rotating machinery at idle. Sequence A must establish the pressurized hot-gas path.

title: From Air Search to Engagement Assessment
headline: Order the information and authorization chain in a layered defensive response.
kicker: Task-group operations room · An uncorrelated air contact approaches
story: A surveillance sensor reports a new contact. The force must transform an uncertain return into a shared track, assess identity and intent, select a proportionate response, and determine whether the threat remains.
Arrange the high-level decision chain without assuming that detection automatically authorizes engagement.
overview: A defensive system is a chain of evidence and control. Sensors create measurements; trackers create state estimates; identification combines cooperative, intelligence, and behavioral evidence; command evaluates rules and risk; weapons or countermeasures require a quality solution; and assessment closes the loop.
terms: A sensor-level observation from one scan or report.
A time-linked estimate of position, velocity, and uncertainty.
Assessment of whether a contact is friendly, neutral, unknown, or hostile.
Determining whether reports from different sensors describe the same object.
Accuracy and update rate sufficient for a selected engagement system.
Command permission under applicable rules and delegated authority.
Evaluation of whether the action achieved the intended effect.
note: The puzzle stays at public, system-level concepts. Real engagement criteria, ranges, tactics, and authorities depend on mission and classification.
sources: Fact-checked against public naval radar, command-and-control, identification, and layered-defense concepts.

cards: A surveillance sensor generates an uncorrelated plot
Successive plots initiate a tentative track
Other sensor reports are correlated with that track
The fused track gains a better position, velocity, and uncertainty estimate
Cooperative, intelligence, and behavior evidence support identification
Command evaluates intent, rules, geometry, and risk
The force selects a warning, maneuver, countermeasure, or engagement option
The responsible authority approves the selected action
Sensors maintain the quality required by the chosen system
Sensors observe the contact and action effects
The force assesses whether the threat is removed or another layer is required

segues: A common operating picture now contains a refined track. The next dependency is judgment: identity, intent, authority, and proportional response must be established before action.
The action has been authorized. Execution still depends on adequate track quality, and the defensive cycle is not complete until sensors determine what changed.
principles: A measurement is not a decision
Sensor evidence must be tracked, correlated, and interpreted before command action.
Identity and intent are separate questions
A known platform can still behave unexpectedly; an unknown contact is not automatically hostile.
Authority is load-bearing
A technically possible action may remain prohibited or inappropriate.
Assessment closes the loop
Defensive systems must observe outcomes and decide whether another response is needed.
hints: Successive plots must first initiate a track before reports from other sensors can be correlated to it.
Authorization comes before execution, while assessment comes only after effects can be observed.
intro: Only one sensor has reported the contact. Sequence A must turn isolated measurements into a refined shared track before identification and command judgment can proceed.
